glossary.Symmetrical polyarthritis: Inflammation of many joints affecting both sides of the body equally.
glossary.Rheumatoid nodules: Firm, painless lumps under the skin, often over the elbows, seen in seropositive RA.
glossary.Insidious onset: Symptoms that start gradually and subtly rather than suddenly.
glossary.Prognosis: The likely course and outcome of a disease.
glossary.Modifiable risk factor: A risk factor the patient can change, such as smoking.
glossary.Inflammatory stiffness: Stiffness worst after rest and in the morning that eases with movement.
glossary.Flare: A period when disease activity suddenly worsens.
glossary.Malaise: A general feeling of being unwell.
glossary.Pulmonary hypertension: Raised blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs.
glossary.Cervical cord compression: Pressure on the spinal cord in the neck, causing limb weakness and sensory loss.
glossary.Ischaemic heart disease: Heart disease caused by narrowed coronary arteries reducing blood supply to the heart muscle.
glossary.Exudative pleural effusion: Protein-rich fluid around the lung caused by inflammation or malignancy.
glossary.Pneumoconiosis: Lung disease caused by inhaling mineral dusts such as coal, asbestos or silica.
glossary.Intrapulmonary nodules: Small round lesions within the lung tissue.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.IgM: Large antibody class made early in immune responses; RF is usually IgM.
glossary.IgG: The most common antibody class in the blood.
glossary.Fc portion: The tail end of an antibody that binds immune cells and complement.
glossary.Autoantibody: An antibody directed against the body's own tissues.
glossary.Immune complex: A clump of antibody bound to its antigen that can deposit in tissues and cause inflammation.
glossary.Joint space narrowing: Loss of the gap between bones on X-ray, reflecting cartilage loss.
glossary.Prednisolone: An oral corticosteroid used to dampen inflammation quickly.
glossary.Folate antagonist: A drug that blocks the use of folate, which cells need to make DNA.
glossary.Macrocytic anaemia: Anaemia with abnormally large red blood cells, for example from folate deficiency.
glossary.eGFR: Estimated glomerular filtration rate, a measure of kidney function.
glossary.Sulfonamide allergy: Allergy to sulfa-containing drugs, which rules out sulfasalazine.
glossary.Conventional DMARD: A traditional small-molecule disease-modifying drug such as methotrexate, as opposed to a biologic.
glossary.Remission: A period with no or minimal signs of disease activity.
glossary.Biologic therapy: Drugs made from living cells, usually antibodies, that block a specific immune target.
glossary.Infliximab: An intravenous monoclonal antibody that blocks TNF-alpha.
glossary.Etanercept: An injectable fusion protein that mops up TNF-alpha.
glossary.Adalimumab: A subcutaneous monoclonal antibody that blocks TNF-alpha.
glossary.Latent TB: Dormant TB infection without symptoms, which can reactivate when immunity is suppressed.
glossary.Washout period: Time allowed after stopping a drug for it to leave the body before, for example, conception.
glossary.Intramuscular: Given by injection into a muscle.
glossary.Cytokines: Small signalling proteins that immune cells use to drive inflammation.
glossary.TNF-alpha: Tumour necrosis factor alpha, a key pro-inflammatory cytokine in RA.
glossary.IL-6: Interleukin-6, a cytokine driving inflammation and the acute-phase response.
glossary.IL-1: Interleukin-1, a pro-inflammatory cytokine causing fever and joint inflammation.
glossary.Hyperplastic: Overgrown through an increased number of cells.
glossary.T cell: A white blood cell that directs or carries out immune attacks.
glossary.Immunogenic: Able to provoke an immune response.
glossary.Functional hyposplenism: A spleen that is present but does not work properly to fight infection.
glossary.Cartilage: Smooth tissue covering the ends of bones inside a joint.
